Reference: Gardner et al. (2024)

Model Setting

The paper develops a regression-based framework for estimation and inference in difference-in-differences (DD) designs with staggered treatment adoption and heterogeneous treatment effects. Its starting point is that the usual two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression is misspecified in this setting: under parallel trends, mean outcomes are linear in group effects, period effects and treatment status only if average treatment effects are the same for every group and period. The proposed two-stage difference-in-differences (2SDD) estimator exploits the fact that untreated outcomes are always linear in group and period effects. The first stage regresses outcomes on group and period fixed effects using untreated observations only, and the second stage regresses outcomes net of the estimated fixed effects on treatment status. The procedure identifies the overall average effect of the treatment on the treated, and with other second-stage regressors it identifies duration-specific effects, pre-treatment placebo coefficients and group- or period-specific effects. Because both stages are regressions, the estimator is a joint generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator, which gives analytical standard errors that account for the first-stage estimation without bootstrapping and without estimating group-specific effects or variances.

The paper has three parts. Section 2 motivates the estimator in a simple setting with group and period effects, and Section 3 gives the asymptotic theory in a general setting with unit fixed effects and covariates, together with extensions (weaker parallel trends, triple differences, serial correlation, continuous treatments, anticipation, reversible treatments, design-based interpretation). Section 4 extends the placebo-law simulations of Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004) to heterogeneous effects and staggered timing with state-level wage data: 2SDD has rejection rates near 5 percent and standard errors near 0.10, while the default variance of the numerically identical imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) over-rejects (13 to 17 percent) and other robust estimators have standard errors that are 30 to 60 percent larger. With homogeneous effects 2SDD is almost as precise as TWFE. Section 5 reanalyses seven published applications and finds that 2SDD has the fewest outlying standard errors and the lowest rate of extreme ttt-statistics. The copy of the paper used for this note ends with the main tables, so the appendices (Stata syntax, the derivation of the TWFE weights and the proofs, the fixed-design discussion, the stacked estimator) are described here only through what the main text says about them.

This closed form for the residualized treatment requires a balanced panel, in which group and period shares are independent. The representation follows from Theorem 1 of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020), and the paper's appendix derives it by population regression algebra. The logic is the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem: the coefficient equals the coefficient from regressing YgpitY_{gpit}Ygpit​ on the residual from a regression of treatment status on group and period effects, and for a treated cell that residual is the bracketed term in ω~gp\tilde{\omega}_{gp}ω~gp​. The weights sum to one, ω11=1\omega_{11}=1ω11​=1 when there is a single treated group, and some weights can be negative. The interpretation is that the misspecified regression attributes part of the treatment effects to the estimated fixed effects: the longer a group is treated (the larger Pr⁡(Dgp=1∣g)\Pr(D_{gp}=1\mid g)Pr(Dgp​=1∣g)), the more of its effects are absorbed by its group effect, and the more units are treated in a period (the larger Pr⁡(Dgp=1∣p)\Pr(D_{gp}=1\mid p)Pr(Dgp​=1∣p)), the more of that period's effects are absorbed by the period effect. This is the same phenomenon as the use of already-treated units as controls for newly treated ones.

The Two-Stage Estimator

Since the problem is misspecification of the outcome model for treated observations, the remedy is to estimate the group and period effects where the model is correct. As long as every group and every period contains untreated observations, λg\lambda_gλg​ and αp\alpha_pαp​ are identified from the untreated subpopulation. The first stage estimates:

Ygpit=λg+αp+ugpit(6)Y_{gpit}=\lambda_g+\alpha_p+u_{gpit} \tag{6}Ygpit​=λg​+αp​+ugpit​(6)

on the sample with Dgp=0D_{gp}=0Dgp​=0 and keeps λ^g\hat{\lambda}_gλ^g​ and α^p\hat{\alpha}_pα^p​. The second stage regresses the adjusted outcome Ygpit−λ^g−α^pY_{gpit}-\hat{\lambda}_g-\hat{\alpha}_pYgpit​−λ^g​−α^p​ on DgpD_{gp}Dgp​. Parallel trends implies:

E[Ygpit∣g,p,Dgp]−λg−αp=E[βgp∣Dgp=1]Dgp+[βgp−E[βgp∣Dgp=1]]Dgp(7)\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{gpit}\mid g,p,D_{gp}\right]-\lambda_g-\alpha_p=\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{gp}\mid D_{gp}=1\right]D_{gp}+\left[\beta_{gp}-\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{gp}\mid D_{gp}=1\right]\right]D_{gp} \tag{7}E[Ygpit​∣g,p,Dgp​]−λg​−αp​=E[βgp​∣Dgp​=1]Dgp​+[βgp​−E[βgp​∣Dgp​=1]]Dgp​(7)

and the last term now has mean zero conditional on DgpD_{gp}Dgp​, the only regressor of the second stage. The second stage therefore identifies E[βgp∣Dgp=1]\mathbb{E}[\beta_{gp}\mid D_{gp}=1]E[βgp​∣Dgp​=1] whatever the pattern of heterogeneity. The first stage is unbiased by standard arguments, and selecting on treatment status creates no sample-selection bias. With PPP fixed the first stage is consistent as the sample grows, and consistency of the second stage follows from the continuous mapping theorem. Time-varying covariates XgpitX_{gpit}Xgpit​ are handled by including them in the first stage and regressing Ygpit−λ^g−α^p−Xgpit′γ^Y_{gpit}-\hat{\lambda}_g-\hat{\alpha}_p-X'_{gpit}\hat{\gamma}Ygpit​−λ^g​−α^p​−Xgpit′​γ^​ on DgpD_{gp}Dgp​ in the second. Treatment effects may then depend arbitrarily on the covariates, but the treatment must not affect the covariates and covariate-specific trends are ruled out unless covariates are interacted with time indicators.

The estimand is the overall average effect on the treated (ATT):

Replacing the duration indicators by group- or period-specific treatment indicators gives group- or period-specific ATTs.

Testing Parallel Trends

The paper compares four pre-trend tests within the two-stage framework. (i) Second-stage leads: the coefficients on WrgpW_{rgp}Wrgp​, r≤0r\leq0r≤0, described above. They are valid tests, but they measure average first-stage residuals and not average deviations from trend. (ii) First-stage leads: Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) include leads of treatment in the first stage, where inference is ordinary least squares and, under some conditions, conditioning on passing the test does not distort the later estimates. These coefficients presumably identify a possibly non-convex weighted average of deviations from trend, come from a different regression than the post-treatment coefficients and are not directly comparable to them. (iii) Placebo ATTs: assume that parallel trends holds up to K+1K+1K+1 periods before adoption and estimate the KKK pre-treatment placebo effects for r∈{−K,…,−1}r\in\{-K,\ldots,-1\}r∈{−K,…,−1} with the two-stage procedure (also Liu, Wang and Xu 2022). (iv) Restricted first stage: estimate the first stage on all observations of never-treated units, which identify the period effects, and on the last pre-treatment period of eventually-treated units, which identifies their group effects. Under the normalization that parallel trends holds in the last pre-treatment period, the same normalization as in a TWFE event study, the second-stage coefficients on the leads then identify average pre-treatment deviations of eventually-treated units from never-treated trends. The restriction costs efficiency, but an appendix figure shows that it recovers both pre- and post-treatment paths in the example of Roth (2024) in which the default versions of several robust estimators do not, and it can perform better when the gap between eventually- and never-treated units widens over time. When parallel trends fails, the first- and second-stage coefficients identify different parameters, although both are zero when it holds.

Inference: Joint GMM

The second-stage dependent variable is generated from first-stage estimates, so ordinary second-stage standard errors are invalid. One option is to bootstrap both stages. The paper's approach treats the two stages as one joint GMM estimator. Let Zgpit=[Ygpit,(1(g)gpit),(1(p)gpit),Dgp]Z_{gpit}=[Y_{gpit},(1(g)_{gpit}),(1(p)_{gpit}),D_{gp}]Zgpit​=[Ygpit​,(1(g)gpit​),(1(p)gpit​),Dgp​] collect the outcome, the GGG-vector of group indicators, the PPP-vector of period indicators and treatment status, and let λ\lambdaλ and α\alphaα be the vectors of group and period effects. The estimator solves the sample analog of:

E[f(λ,α,β;Zgpit)]=E[[Ygpit−(1(g)gpit)′λ−(1(p)gpit)′α][(1(g)gpit),(1(p)gpit)]′(1−Dgp)[Ygpit−(1(g)gpit)′λ−(1(p)gpit)′α−βDgp]Dgp]=0(13)\mathbb{E}\left[f(\lambda,\alpha,\beta;Z_{gpit})\right]=\mathbb{E}\begin{bmatrix}\left[Y_{gpit}-(1(g)_{gpit})'\lambda-(1(p)_{gpit})'\alpha\right]\left[(1(g)_{gpit}),(1(p)_{gpit})\right]'(1-D_{gp})\\ \left[Y_{gpit}-(1(g)_{gpit})'\lambda-(1(p)_{gpit})'\alpha-\beta D_{gp}\right]D_{gp}\end{bmatrix}=0 \tag{13}E[f(λ,α,β;Zgpit​)]=E[[Ygpit​−(1(g)gpit​)′λ−(1(p)gpit​)′α][(1(g)gpit​),(1(p)gpit​)]′(1−Dgp​)[Ygpit​−(1(g)gpit​)′λ−(1(p)gpit​)′α−βDgp​]Dgp​​]=0(13)

(the paper writes WgpitW_{gpit}Wgpit​ for the data on the left-hand side). The first block is the set of normal equations of the first stage on untreated observations and the last row is the normal equation of the second stage. The system is just identified. By Theorem 6.1 of Newey and McFadden (1994) on sequential estimators, N(β^−β)\sqrt{N}(\hat{\beta}-\beta)N​(β^​−β) is asymptotically N(0,v)\mathcal{N}(0,v)N(0,v), where vvv is the last diagonal element of:

E[∂f(λ,α,β;Zgpit)∂(λ,α,β)]−1E[f(λ,α,β;Zgpit)f(λ,α,β;Zgpit)′]E[∂f(λ,α,β;Zgpit)∂(λ,α,β)]−1′(14)\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial f(\lambda,\alpha,\beta;Z_{gpit})}{\partial(\lambda,\alpha,\beta)}\right]^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[f(\lambda,\alpha,\beta;Z_{gpit})f(\lambda,\alpha,\beta;Z_{gpit})'\right]\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial f(\lambda,\alpha,\beta;Z_{gpit})}{\partial(\lambda,\alpha,\beta)}\right]^{-1\prime} \tag{14}E[∂(λ,α,β)∂f(λ,α,β;Zgpit​)​]−1E[f(λ,α,β;Zgpit​)f(λ,α,β;Zgpit​)′]E[∂(λ,α,β)∂f(λ,α,β;Zgpit​)​]−1′(14)

The Jacobian is block triangular, because the second-stage moment depends on (λ,α)(\lambda,\alpha)(λ,α) while the first-stage moments do not depend on β\betaβ, and its off-diagonal block carries the first-stage sampling error into the variance of β^\hat{\beta}β^​. In practice both stages are passed to a GMM routine, or the second-stage variance is corrected manually with this expression. In contrast to methods that average cohort-specific estimates, neither estimation nor inference involves group-specific treatment effects.

Extensions

  • Weaker parallel trends: the theory assumes parallel trends for every group and every pair of consecutive periods, as in de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020) and Sun and Abraham (2021). Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) require it only between treated and never-treated groups after treatment. The weaker version is accommodated by using only never-treated groups in the first stage, at a cost in power. Conversely, when the stronger version holds, the Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator does not gain precision, because it does not use treated units' observations before relative time −1-1−1.

  • Violations of parallel trends: if trends differ and the gap grows over time, bias is reduced by estimating the first stage on untreated observations within a few periods of treatment, or by adding group-specific linear trends 1{g(i)=g}t1\{g(i)=g\}t1{g(i)=g}t to XitX_{it}Xit​, where g(i)g(i)g(i) is the group of unit iii.

  • Triple differences: the additional treatment, time and group indicators are collected in XitX_{it}Xit​, and the two steps are unchanged.

  • Serial correlation: because the estimator coincides with the imputation estimator, it is efficient in the normal homoskedastic model. If εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​ is AR(1) with parameter ρ\rhoρ, the model can be written as:

    Yit=ρYit−1+δitDit+λ~i+γ~t+νit,νit∣Dit,Yit−1∼N(0,σ2)(25)Y_{it}=\rho Y_{it-1}+\delta_{it}D_{it}+\tilde{\lambda}_i+\tilde{\gamma}_t+\nu_{it},\qquad\nu_{it}\mid D_{it},Y^{t-1}_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2) \tag{25}Yit​=ρYit−1​+δit​Dit​+λ~i​+γ~​t​+νit​,νit​∣Dit​,Yit−1​∼N(0,σ2)(25)

    with Yit−1≡{Yi1,…,Yit−1}Y^{t-1}_i\equiv\{Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{it-1}\}Yit−1​≡{Yi1​,…,Yit−1​}. The first stage regresses YitY_{it}Yit​ on Yit−1Y_{it-1}Yit−1​, XitX_{it}Xit​ and fixed effects for untreated observations, and the second regresses Yit−ρ^Yit−1−λ~^i−γ~^tY_{it}-\hat{\rho}Y_{it-1}-\hat{\tilde{\lambda}}_i-\hat{\tilde{\gamma}}_tYit​−ρ^​Yit−1​−λ~^i​−γ~​^​t​ on DitD_{it}Dit​. The result is efficient because least squares is maximum likelihood, but the estimand δit\delta_{it}δit​ is a different one.

  • Continuous treatments: if Dit=0D_{it}=0Dit​=0 before treatment and takes continuous or multiple values afterwards, the same two stages identify a positively weighted average of derivatives of the causal response function (Yitzhaki 1996).

  • Anticipation and reversible treatments: if the treatment is anticipated rrr periods ahead, the definition of treated is shifted by rrr periods. For reversible or multiple treatments, WitW_{it}Wit​ becomes a vector of indicators for treatment paths (the sequence of treatment states since first treatment), observations after first treatment are excluded from the first stage, and coefficients are effects relative to the untreated state.

  • Design-based interpretation: let AiA_iAi​ be the number of treated periods of unit iii and assume βit=βi\beta_{it}=\beta_iβit​=βi​. If adoption timing is as good as random as in Athey and Imbens (2022), with E[Ai]=a\mathbb{E}[A_i]=aE[Ai​]=a for all iii, then:

    β=1aNE[∑i=1NAiβi]=1aN∑i=1NE[Ai]βi=1N∑i=1Nβi(26)\beta=\frac{1}{aN}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^NA_i\beta_i\right]=\frac{1}{aN}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{E}[A_i]\beta_i=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\beta_i \tag{26}β=aN1​E[i=1∑N​Ai​βi​]=aN1​i=1∑N​E[Ai​]βi​=N1​i=1∑N​βi​(26)

    so the estimand is the average treatment effect.

  • Linear combinations: for nonstochastic weights witw_{it}wit​, let E[Dit]=1(h)it′ζ\mathbb{E}[D_{it}]=1(h)'_{it}\zetaE[Dit​]=1(h)it′​ζ, where 1(h)it1(h)_{it}1(h)it​ are indicators of the level hhh at which the treatment probability varies and ζ\zetaζ is known or consistently estimable with nonzero elements. Then:

    τ=∑i,twitβit=∑i,twitE[Yit−Xit′γ1(h)it′ζ](27)\tau=\sum_{i,t}w_{it}\beta_{it}=\sum_{i,t}w_{it}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y_{it}-X'_{it}\gamma}{1(h)'_{it}\zeta}\right] \tag{27}τ=i,t∑​wit​βit​=i,t∑​wit​E[1(h)it′​ζYit​−Xit′​γ​](27)

    and ζ\zetaζ, γ\gammaγ and τ\tauτ are estimated jointly from a just-identified system of moment conditions. The paper first defines τ\tauτ as witβitw_{it}\beta_{it}wit​βit​ without the sum.

Relation to Other Estimators

  • Imputation: the point estimates are numerically identical to those of the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024), and of the estimators of Liu, Wang and Xu and of Thakral and To. The paper states this identity without a separate theorem; the formal equivalence it argues is the one with the saturated TWFE regression above. The efficiency result of Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess under homoskedastic normal errors therefore carries over. The difference lies in inference. With vitv_{it}vit​ the weight on the residual of observation (i,t)(i,t)(i,t), τ^it\hat{\tau}_{it}τ^it​ the estimated effect used by the imputation variance and τ^\hat{\tau}τ^ the overall estimate, the two variance estimators are:

    σ^BJS2=∑i(∑tvit(Yit−Xit′γ^−Ditτ^it))2σ^2SDD2=∑i(∑tvit(Yit−Xit′γ^−Ditτ^))2=σ^BJS2+∑i(∑tvitDit(τ^it−τ^))2+2∑i(∑tvitDit(τ^it−τ^))(∑tvit(Yit−Xit′γ^−Ditτ^it))(28)\begin{aligned} \hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{BJS}}&=\sum_i\left(\sum_tv_{it}\left(Y_{it}-X'_{it}\hat{\gamma}-D_{it}\hat{\tau}_{it}\right)\right)^2\\ \hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{2SDD}}&=\sum_i\left(\sum_tv_{it}\left(Y_{it}-X'_{it}\hat{\gamma}-D_{it}\hat{\tau}\right)\right)^2\\ &=\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{BJS}}+\sum_i\left(\sum_tv_{it}D_{it}\left(\hat{\tau}_{it}-\hat{\tau}\right)\right)^2+2\sum_i\left(\sum_tv_{it}D_{it}\left(\hat{\tau}_{it}-\hat{\tau}\right)\right)\left(\sum_tv_{it}\left(Y_{it}-X'_{it}\hat{\gamma}-D_{it}\hat{\tau}_{it}\right)\right) \end{aligned} \tag{28}σ^BJS2​σ^2SDD2​​=i∑​(t∑​vit​(Yit​−Xit′​γ^​−Dit​τ^it​))2=i∑​(t∑​vit​(Yit​−Xit′​γ^​−Dit​τ^))2=σ^BJS2​+i∑​(t∑​vit​Dit​(τ^it​−τ^))2+2i∑​(t∑​vit​Dit​(τ^it​−τ^))(t∑​vit​(Yit​−Xit′​γ^​−Dit​τ^it​))​(28)

    The last line is the exact expansion of the square. The paper prints the cross term without the factor 2 and with τ^\hat{\tau}τ^ in place of τ^it\hat{\tau}_{it}τ^it​ in its second factor, which is not an identity. The imputation variance exceeds the 2SDD variance only when the cross term is negative enough. Its default uses cohort-by-period averages of estimated effects for τ^it\hat{\tau}_{it}τ^it​. With small cohorts these averages overfit, the residuals shrink toward zero and the variance is understated, the more so the more cohorts there are relative to NNN. The leave-out version corrects this but cannot be computed when a cohort has a single unit. GMM in effect uses the coarsest average, τ^=β^\hat{\tau}=\hat{\beta}τ^=β^​.

  • Cohort-averaging estimators: Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021), Sun and Abraham (2021) and de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020, 2024) estimate group-specific effects and aggregate them. They estimate group effects or variances separately, the first relies on the bootstrap in its implementation, and precision falls with many or small cohorts.

  • Stacked regressions: stacking cohort-specific datasets identifies a weighted average of group-specific effects with weights that depend on the relative sizes of the stacked datasets and on the variance of treatment within them (shown in an appendix). It requires a fixed event window and a balanced panel, and reuses controls across stacks without a theory of inference.

  • Extended TWFE: the approach of Wooldridge (2021) considers only time-invariant covariates and assumes that treatment effects are linear in covariates.

  • TWFE under homogeneity: when βit=β\beta_{it}=\betaβit​=β both first stages are consistent for the fixed effects, so TWFE and 2SDD converge to the same limit and differ only in the second stage, where TWFE regresses the residualized outcome on residualized treatment and 2SDD regresses it on DitD_{it}Dit​. The cost of robustness is therefore only a difference in variance, which the simulations show to be small.

Simulation Evidence

The data are log weekly earnings of women aged 25 to 50 in the Current Population Survey outgoing rotation groups, 1979 to 2020, more than one million women, collapsed to 2,100 state-by-year cells for 50 states and 42 years. A second dataset draws the outcome independently from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance. The design is random: each replication draws the treated states, the treatment years (between 1982 and 2014, so that at least five post-treatment years are observed) and the treatment effects. In the baseline, 40 states are treated over 20 years with two states per year, and effects are normal with a mean drawn uniformly between 2 and 5 percent of the average wage and a standard deviation of 10 percent of the average wage, so the average true effect is about 0.2. Event-study effects are estimated for the five years starting with the year of treatment (periods 0 to 4), standard errors are clustered by state, and the criterion is the frequency with which the true effect is rejected at the 5 percent level (the text reports 500 replications and the table notes 501).

  • Baseline: 2SDD rejects in 4.6 to 5.8 percent of replications, with average standard errors of 0.103 to 0.105, bias of at most 0.0075 in absolute value and root-mean-square error of 0.100 to 0.105. The imputation estimator with default variance rejects in 13.0 to 16.8 percent (standard errors 0.074 to 0.077), and with leave-out variance in 0.4 to 1.8 percent (0.141 to 0.143). Callaway and Sant'Anna reject in 3.0 to 5.4 percent (0.142 to 0.144), Sun and Abraham in 0.6 to 1.8 percent (0.167 to 0.168), de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille in 5.0 to 6.6 percent (0.137 to 0.139) and Wooldridge in 4.2 to 6.8 percent (0.134 to 0.136). The root-mean-square errors of these four are 0.127 to 0.143. Average computing time per replication is 0.10 seconds for 2SDD and 0.20 for imputation, against 3.6, 31, 47 and 88 seconds for de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille, Callaway and Sant'Anna, Sun and Abraham, and Wooldridge.

  • More cohorts: with 40 states treated over 30 years (at least one per year), 2SDD rejects in 3.8 to 7.0 percent with standard errors of 0.101 to 0.104. The default imputation variance rejects in 25.3 to 29.7 percent (standard errors 0.055 to 0.057), de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille in 18.0 to 23.0 percent (0.092 to 0.097) and Wooldridge in 10.0 to 12.4 percent (0.116 to 0.121). Callaway and Sant'Anna remain near 5 percent (0.140 to 0.142) and Sun and Abraham under-reject (1.2 to 2.0 percent, 0.165 to 0.169). The leave-out variance cannot be computed. With 15 cohorts the default imputation variance still rejects in about 10 to 12 percent.

  • Fewer treated states: going from 40 to 30 treated states with 15 cohorts raises standard errors and leaves rejection rates stable for all methods except the default imputation variance and Wooldridge.

  • Homogeneous effects: with a common effect equal to 5 percent of the average wage, a TWFE regression that imposes zero pre-treatment effects and 2SDD both reject in about 5 percent, with average standard errors of 0.102 and 0.103; the fully dynamic TWFE specification has 0.137. The default imputation standard error is about 25 percent smaller than that of TWFE and rejects about three times as often. The leave-out version (0.14) and Sun and Abraham (0.17) reject only 20 to 40 percent as often as TWFE, and the other three have correct rejection rates with standard errors of 0.13 to 0.14.

  • Independent data: in the baseline design with independent outcomes, 2SDD rejects in 4.4 to 5.2 percent with standard errors of 0.129 to 0.131. In the table, the default imputation variance rejects in 14.6 to 16.8 percent (0.094 to 0.097) and the leave-out version in 0.6 to 1.4 percent (0.176 to 0.180); the text reports slightly wider ranges. Callaway and Sant'Anna, de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille, and Wooldridge are close to 5 percent with standard errors of 0.168 to 0.180, about 30 percent above 2SDD, and Sun and Abraham under-reject (0.209 to 0.210). With more cohorts, rejection rates reach 31.7, 21.2 and 13.2 percent for the default imputation variance, de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille, and Wooldridge.

Empirical Applications

The paper replicates the papers with staggered timing and a single treatment listed in Table 1 of Sun and Abraham (2021): Tewari (2014; 39 states, 1976 to 2007, 20 cohorts), Ujhelyi (2014; 48 states, 1960 to 1984, 21 cohorts), Bailey and Goodman-Bacon (2015; 3,062 counties, 1959 to 1998), Deryugina (2017; 1,183 counties, 1969 to 2012, 15 cohorts), He and Wang (2017; 255 villages, 2000 to 2011, 8 cohorts), Lafortune, Rothstein and Schanzenbach (2018; 49 states, 1990 to 2014, 18 cohorts) and Kuziemko, Meckel and Rossin-Slater (2018; 250 counties, 1993 to 2001, 5 cohorts). The last is treated separately because treatment timing is monthly and outcomes are yearly, so six settings enter the main comparisons. For Bailey and Goodman-Bacon the list of applications reports 9 cohorts and the text 15. Five estimators are compared (2SDD, imputation with default variance, Callaway and Sant'Anna, Sun and Abraham, de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille). True effects are unknown, so the comparison concerns agreement across methods. Point estimates are similar across the robust estimators and differ from TWFE.

  • Standard errors relative to 2SDD: regressions of standard errors on method indicators give, for Callaway and Sant'Anna, a difference of 516.4 (standard error 272.8) in Bailey and Goodman-Bacon, against 7.3 for imputation, −2.9-2.9−2.9 for Sun and Abraham and 0.7 for de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille; in that application the imputation standard error is in some cases more than twice that of 2SDD. In Lafortune, Rothstein and Schanzenbach the imputation difference is −172.0-172.0−172.0 (11.5): its standard errors are about half those of the other methods, and it alone finds significant increases in transfers to the highest-income districts. In Tewari the Sun and Abraham difference is −0.0104-0.0104−0.0104 (0.0008), and its estimates switch between significantly positive and significantly negative. The imputation standard error is smaller than that of 2SDD in five of the six settings. Callaway and Sant'Anna is least precise with many groups, while Sun and Abraham and de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille are precise with many groups and do worse with many small cohorts.

  • Outliers: each standard error and each ttt-statistic is compared with the mean over the other four methods for the same coefficient. 2SDD has the fewest outliers in the top and bottom 2.5 percent, and its outlying standard errors are mostly conservative. Relative to 2SDD, absolute ttt-statistics are higher by 0.51 for imputation, 0.92 for Sun and Abraham and 0.51 for de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille, and lower by 0.29 for Callaway and Sant'Anna. The share of coefficients with ∣t∣>1.96|t|>1.96∣t∣>1.96 differs by 7.6, 8.8, 10.7 and −8.2-8.2−8.2 percentage points, and the share above the 90th percentile of the pooled distribution (about 4.3) by 9.8, 11.6, 9.5 and −1.2-1.2−1.2 percentage points.

  • Horizon and pre-periods: standard errors of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille grow significantly faster with time since treatment than those of 2SDD in four settings. Only 2SDD yields the full set of dynamic estimates in Tewari. Differences between 2SDD and imputation in pre-event coefficients reflect the choice between second-stage and first-stage leads, not a difference in method.

  • TWFE: for nearly one-sixth of dynamic estimates the TWFE conclusion (significantly positive, significantly negative or insignificant) agrees with none of the robust estimators. In about 40 percent of these cases all robust estimates are significant with the same sign and TWFE is insignificant. The authors conclude that 2SDD should replace TWFE as the default for dynamic effects under staggered timing.

The starting point is the potential-outcome form of the observed outcome and the parallel trends assumption. The observed outcome is the untreated outcome plus the treatment effect when treated:

Ygpit=Ygpit(d=0)+Dgp[Ygpit(d=1)−Ygpit(d=0)].Y_{gpit}=Y_{gpit}(d=0)+D_{gp}\left[Y_{gpit}(d=1)-Y_{gpit}(d=0)\right].Ygpit​=Ygpit​(d=0)+Dgp​[Ygpit​(d=1)−Ygpit​(d=0)].

Parallel trends says that mean untreated outcomes are additive in a group effect and a period effect, for every group and period, whether or not the cell is treated:

E[Ygpit(d=0)∣g,p]=λg+αp.\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{gpit}(d=0)\mid g,p\right]=\lambda_g+\alpha_p.E[Ygpit​(d=0)∣g,p]=λg​+αp​.

Since DgpD_{gp}Dgp​ is a function of (g,p)(g,p)(g,p), conditioning on it adds nothing. Taking the conditional expectation of the first line and using the definition βgp=E[Ygpit(d=1)−Ygpit(d=0)∣g,p]\beta_{gp}=\mathbb{E}[Y_{gpit}(d=1)-Y_{gpit}(d=0)\mid g,p]βgp​=E[Ygpit​(d=1)−Ygpit​(d=0)∣g,p]:

E[Ygpit∣g,p,Dgp]=E[Ygpit(d=0)∣g,p]+Dgp E[Ygpit(d=1)−Ygpit(d=0)∣g,p]=λg+αp+βgpDgp.\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[Y_{gpit}\mid g,p,D_{gp}\right]&=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{gpit}(d=0)\mid g,p\right]+D_{gp}\,\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{gpit}(d=1)-Y_{gpit}(d=0)\mid g,p\right]\\ &=\lambda_g+\alpha_p+\beta_{gp}D_{gp}. \end{aligned}E[Ygpit​∣g,p,Dgp​]​=E[Ygpit​(d=0)∣g,p]+Dgp​E[Ygpit​(d=1)−Ygpit​(d=0)∣g,p]=λg​+αp​+βgp​Dgp​.​

The name comes from the implication for untreated trends: E[Y(d=0)∣g,p]−E[Y(d=0)∣g,p−1]=αp−αp−1\mathbb{E}[Y(d=0)\mid g,p]-\mathbb{E}[Y(d=0)\mid g,p-1]=\alpha_p-\alpha_{p-1}E[Y(d=0)∣g,p]−E[Y(d=0)∣g,p−1]=αp​−αp−1​ is the same for every group. No anticipation is what allows βgpDgp\beta_{gp}D_{gp}βgp​Dgp​ to vanish before adoption.

This is the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression that the paper criticizes: the outcome is regressed on a full set of group indicators (coefficients λg\lambda_gλg​), period indicators (αp\alpha_pαp​) and the treatment dummy DgpD_{gp}Dgp​, with a single coefficient β\betaβ and a regression error εgpit\varepsilon_{gpit}εgpit​. Compared with equation (1) the only change is that the cell-specific effect βgp\beta_{gp}βgp​ is replaced by one number.

With two groups and two periods (G=P=1G=P=1G=P=1) only the cell (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) is treated, equation (1) has four cell means and four parameters, and the regression is saturated. Its coefficient is the classical double difference

β=(E[Y∣1,1]−E[Y∣1,0])−(E[Y∣0,1]−E[Y∣0,0])=β11,\beta=\left(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid 1,1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid 1,0]\right)-\left(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid 0,1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid 0,0]\right)=\beta_{11},β=(E[Y∣1,1]−E[Y∣1,0])−(E[Y∣0,1]−E[Y∣0,0])=β11​,

where the first difference removes λ1\lambda_1λ1​ and the second removes α1−α0\alpha_1-\alpha_0α1​−α0​. Identification comes from the change over time in the treated group relative to the change in the untreated group.

Replacing group and period effects by unit and time effects does not change the coefficient: by the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem it depends on the regressors only through the residual of DgpD_{gp}Dgp​ on the fixed effects, and DgpD_{gp}Dgp​ varies only by group and period. With more groups and periods the regression is no longer saturated; equations (3) to (5) show what its coefficient then is, and equation (6) starts the remedy.

Start from equation (1) and add and subtract the target parameter E[βgp∣Dgp=1]\mathbb{E}[\beta_{gp}\mid D_{gp}=1]E[βgp​∣Dgp​=1] multiplied by DgpD_{gp}Dgp​:

This is the outcome model of the general theory. Because TTT is fixed, the time indicators are then absorbed into XitX_{it}Xit​, so in the later equations αt\alpha_tαt​ is part of Xit′γX'_{it}\gammaXit′​γ.

The second line is strict exogeneity: the error at ttt is mean independent of the whole path of treatment and covariates of the unit, not only of their values at ttt. Together the two lines are the parallel trends assumption, since for an untreated observation

Strict exogeneity also rules out anticipation and adoption timing that responds to past shocks, for example adopting after a bad draw of εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​. Nothing is assumed about the correlation of λi\lambda_iλi​ with treatment timing, about serial correlation or heteroskedasticity of εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​, or about βit\beta_{it}βit​ beyond finite second moments. The effect βit\beta_{it}βit​ may depend on covariates, but the treatment must not change XitX_{it}Xit​.

That expression would give ∑iai2+2∑ibi2+∑iaibi\sum_ia_i^2+2\sum_ib_i^2+\sum_ia_ib_i∑i​ai2​+2∑i​bi2​+∑i​ai​bi​, which differs from (ai+bi)2(a_i+b_i)^2(ai​+bi​)2 summed over iii by ∑ibi2−∑iaibi\sum_ib_i^2-\sum_ia_ib_i∑i​bi2​−∑i​ai​bi​, so it is not an identity. An equivalent correct form with the paper's second factor is

σ^2SDD2=σ^BJS2−∑ibi2+2∑ibi(ai+bi).\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{2SDD}}=\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{BJS}}-\sum_ib_i^2+2\sum_ib_i\left(a_i+b_i\right).σ^2SDD2​=σ^BJS2​−i∑​bi2​+2i∑​bi​(ai​+bi​).

Consequence: σ^BJS2>σ^2SDD2\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{BJS}}>\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{2SDD}}σ^BJS2​>σ^2SDD2​ if and only if ∑ibi2+2∑iaibi<0\sum_ib_i^2+2\sum_ia_ib_i<0∑i​bi2​+2∑i​ai​bi​<0, that is, the cross term must be negative and larger in absolute value than ∑ibi2≥0\sum_ib_i^2\geq0∑i​bi2​≥0. Otherwise the imputation variance is the smaller one. This is the typical case when τ^it\hat{\tau}_{it}τ^it​ is a cohort-by-period average over few units: such averages fit the treated residuals closely, aia_iai​ shrinks and the variance is understated. The 2SDD residual subtracts only the single overall estimate τ^=β^\hat{\tau}=\hat{\beta}τ^=β^​, so treatment-effect heterogeneity stays in the residual, as it does in ggg of equation (21).
